questions.question: Pens are bought at 10 for ₹40 and sold at 6 for ₹30. Find the profit %.
questions.answer: CP per pen = 40/10 = ₹4. SP per pen = 30/6 = ₹5. Profit per pen = ₹1. Profit % = (1/4) × 100 % = 25 %.
questions.explanation: Reduce to per-pen CP and SP; then apply the profit-% formula.

questions.question: On a sum of ₹5000 at 10 % p.a. for 2 years, compute the difference between (i) annual compounding, (ii) half-yearly compounding, (iii) simple interest. Comment.
questions.answer: (i) Yearly: A = 5000 · (1.1)^2 = 6050; CI = 1050. (ii) Half-yearly: r/2 = 5 %, n·t = 4 periods. A = 5000 · (1.05)^4 = 5000 · 1.21550625 = 6077.53; CI = 1077.53. (iii) SI: 5000 · 10 · 2 / 100 = 1000. So SI < yearly CI < half-yearly CI. Compounding more often increases the maturity amount; SI is always the smallest because it earns no interest-on-interest.
questions.explanation: Demonstrates the ordering SI ≤ yearly CI ≤ half-yearly CI for the same r and t.

questions.question: Two shops sell the same item: Shop A marks at ₹2000 with successive discounts of 20 % and 10 %; Shop B marks at ₹2000 with a single discount of 28 %. Which is the better deal for the customer?
questions.answer: Shop A: SP = 2000 · 0.80 · 0.90 = 2000 · 0.72 = ₹1440. Shop B: SP = 2000 · 0.72 = ₹1440. Both shops give the same SP. (This is the equivalent-discount calculation: 1 − 0.80 · 0.90 = 0.28 = 28 %.)
questions.explanation: Shows that successive 20 % and 10 % is equivalent to a single 28 % discount, not 30 %.
